---
title: "Matching on the Fly: The Kapelner–Krieger Sequential Designs"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

Pair matching is one of the oldest ways to make a two-arm experiment more precise:
put similar subjects into pairs, then flip a coin within each pair. A matched design
needs every subject's covariates before anyone is assigned. In a clinical trial, a
field experiment or an online test, subjects arrive one at a time, and each must be
assigned when they arrive. The design cannot see who comes next, so it cannot form
the pairs up front.

The usual fallback is to randomize each arrival on its own (a coin flip, or complete
randomization run sequentially). That is valid, but in a small trial chance alone can
leave the two arms noticeably different on an important covariate, and the analysis
pays for that imbalance with a wider interval.

Kapelner and Krieger's *matching on the fly* (Kapelner and Krieger, 2014) keeps the
pairs and gives up the requirement to see everyone first. Each arrival is compared
with the earlier subjects who have not been matched yet. If one of them is close
enough, the two become a pair and the new subject gets the opposite treatment.
Otherwise the new subject is randomized and waits, unmatched, for a later arrival.
EDI (Experimental Design and Inference) implements this design and its extension
(Kapelner and Krieger, 2021) as three classes:

| Class | Distance used to find a match | Acceptance threshold |
|---|---|---|
| `DesignSeqOneByOneKK14` | Mahalanobis distance on all covariates | An F critical value (closed form) |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21` | Weighted squared distance on standardized covariates; weights estimated from the responses so far | A quantile of resampled pairwise distances |
| `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21stepwise` | As KK21, with weights from forward stepwise regression | As KK21 |

This article explains how the three designs work, runs one trial subject by subject,
describes the matched estimator and its inference classes, and measures by simulation
how much the matching gains and when it gains little. It assumes the four steps of an
EDI analysis (design, assign, record responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html)
and the [continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html).

## How the designs work

Every KK design keeps a vector of match labels, one per subject. A label of 0 means
the subject is in the **reservoir**: randomized, and not (yet) matched. A positive
label is a pair number; the two subjects that share it form a matched pair, one
treated and one control. When subject `t` arrives, the design does one of two things:

1. **Match.** Find the reservoir subject closest to subject `t`. If the distance is
   below a threshold, give both the next pair number and assign subject `t` the
   opposite of their partner's treatment. The partner leaves the reservoir.
2. **Randomize.** Otherwise assign subject `t` by a fair coin and add them to the
   reservoir.

Allocation is 1:1 (there is no `prob_T` argument): each pair adds one treated and one
control subject, and reservoir subjects are assigned with probability 1/2. The designs
differ only in how they measure "closest" and what counts as "close enough".

### KK14: Mahalanobis distance and an F threshold

**Burn-in.** For the first `t_0_pct * n` subjects (default `t_0_pct = 0.35`) the
design only randomizes, so that there are enough subjects to estimate the covariance
of the covariates. Every burn-in subject goes into the reservoir.

**Distance.** After burn-in, the design computes the sample covariance matrix $S$ of
the covariates of the subjects seen so far (with a small ridge added for numerical
stability) and, for each reservoir subject $r$, the squared Mahalanobis distance
$$D^2_{t,r} = (x_t - x_r)^\top S^{-1} (x_t - x_r).$$

**Threshold.** The closest reservoir subject is accepted as a match only if
$$D^2_{t,r} < \frac{p\,(n-1)}{n-p}\, F_{p,\; t-p}(\lambda),$$
where $p$ is the rank of the covariate matrix so far, $n$ is the planned sample size,
$t$ is the number of subjects enrolled so far, and $F_{p,\,t-p}(\lambda)$ is the
$\lambda$ quantile of the F distribution with $p$ and $t-p$ degrees of freedom. This
is a Hotelling $T^2$-type test of whether the covariate difference is small. The
argument `lambda` (default 0.1) sets how strict it is: a smaller `lambda` accepts
fewer, closer matches and leaves more subjects in the reservoir.

KK14 uses only the covariates. It never looks at a response, so it gives every
covariate the same importance after the Mahalanobis scaling, including covariates that
have nothing to do with the outcome.

### KK21: weight covariates by how much they predict the response

In most trials some covariates predict the outcome strongly and others not at all.
Matching closely on an irrelevant covariate costs matches and buys no precision.
`DesignSeqOneByOneKK21` learns which covariates matter from the responses collected so
far, so it needs the responses recorded as the trial runs
(`add_one_subject_response()` after each outcome is observed).

**Weights.** At each assignment, for each covariate $j$ separately, KK21 regresses the
responses observed so far on that covariate alone and takes the absolute $t$
statistic (coefficient divided by its standard error) as the raw weight. The model
depends on the response type: OLS for continuous responses, logistic regression for
incidence, and for count, proportion, survival and ordinal responses a fast OLS on a
transformed response by default (on $\log(y+1)$, the logit, $\log(y)$ when nothing is
censored yet, and the numeric level), switchable to a negative binomial, beta, AFT or
proportional-odds fit with the `*_use_speedup` arguments. The weights are normalized to
sum to one; `get_covariate_weights()` returns the latest vector and
`get_iteration_weights()` the whole history.

**Distance.** With standardized covariates $z$ and weights $w_j$, the distance to
reservoir subject $r$ is
$$d^2_{t,r} = \sum_j w_j\, (z_{t,j} - z_{r,j})^2 .$$

**Threshold.** Instead of an F quantile, KK21 draws `num_boot` (default 500) random
pairs of the subjects enrolled so far, computes the same weighted distance for each,
and accepts the closest reservoir subject if its distance is below the `lambda`
quantile (default 10%) of those distances. A match must therefore be closer than about
90% of random pairs.

**Fallback.** Until at least $2(p+2)$ responses are available ($p$ covariates), the
regressions are too unstable to use, and KK21 applies the KK14 rule above. Burn-in
works as in KK14.

### KK21stepwise: weights that account for correlated covariates

KK21's weights are marginal: two correlated covariates that carry the same information
can both get a high weight, which counts that information twice.
`DesignSeqOneByOneKK21stepwise` computes the weights by forward stepwise selection
instead. At each step it fits the response on each remaining covariate together with
the covariates already selected and the treatment indicator, picks the covariate with
the largest absolute association statistic, and uses that statistic as its weight. A
covariate whose information is already captured by earlier selections gets a small
weight. Everything else (burn-in, threshold, matching) is inherited from KK21. Because
the stepwise models include the treatment column, the pairs could in principle depend
on the assignment path; the `condition_on_ws_for_rand_tests` argument controls how the
randomization test handles that (see its help page).

## A worked trial

Sixty subjects arrive one at a time, each with four covariates. The outcome depends
strongly on `x1`, less on `x2`, and not at all on `x3` or `x4`; the treatment adds
`true_effect`. The trial uses KK21 with its defaults, and each response is recorded
as soon as the subject is assigned.

```{r trial-data}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 60
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n), x4 = rnorm(n))
true_effect = 0.5
eps = rnorm(n)
y0 = 1.5 * X$x1 + 1.0 * X$x2 + eps        # response under control
```

```{r trial-run}
des = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
for (t in seq_len(n)) {
  w_t = des$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[t, , drop = FALSE])
  des$add_one_subject_response(t, y0[t] + true_effect * w_t)
}
m = des$get_block_ids()        # match labels: 0 = reservoir, k > 0 = pair k
w = des$get_w()
```

Once all `n` subjects are in, `get_block_ids()` returns the match labels. A pair is
formed when its later member arrives, so the labels also tell us who was waiting in
the reservoir after each arrival: subject `s` was waiting at time `t` if `s <= t` and
`s` is either never matched or matched to someone who arrives after `t`.

```{r trial-reservoir-path}
partner = sapply(seq_len(n), function(s) if (m[s] == 0) NA else setdiff(which(m == m[s]), s))
reservoir_size = sapply(seq_len(n), function(t) {
  s = seq_len(t)
  sum(m[s] == 0 | partner[s] > t)       # TRUE | NA is TRUE for never-matched subjects
})
```

The first `r floor(0.35 * n)` arrivals are burn-in (`t <= t_0_pct * n`), all
randomized into the reservoir; after that, most arrivals find a partner.

```{r trial-pairs}
first_match = which(m > 0 & duplicated(m))[1]       # first arrival that completed a pair
first_match
num_pairs = max(m)
num_reservoir = sum(m == 0)
c(pairs = num_pairs, matched_subjects = 2 * num_pairs, reservoir = num_reservoir)

# the first few pairs: who was matched to whom, and the treatment each got
pair_ids = sort(unique(m[m > 0]))[1:6]
t(sapply(pair_ids, function(k) {
  ij = which(m == k)
  c(pair = k, earlier_subject = ij[1], later_subject = ij[2],
    w_earlier = w[ij[1]], w_later = w[ij[2]])
}))
```

Every pair has one treated and one control subject. The reservoir grew during burn-in
and then shrank as later arrivals drew partners out of it; it held
`r max(reservoir_size)` subjects at its largest and `r num_reservoir` at the end:

```{r trial-reservoir}
reservoir_size[c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60)]
```

The weights at the last assignment put most of the matching effort on `x1` and `x2`,
the two covariates that drive the outcome:

```{r trial-weights}
round(des$get_covariate_weights(), 3)
```

### Balance compared with complete randomization

A single trial says little about balance, because both designs are random. The next
chunk keeps these 60 subjects and their potential outcomes fixed and reruns the
whole trial `n_replay` times under each of three sequential designs: KK14, KK21, and
`DesignSeqOneByOneiBCRD`, complete randomization run sequentially (exactly 30 treated,
with no use of covariates). For each run it records the standardized difference in
means of each covariate between the arms, $(\bar x_T - \bar x_C)/\mathrm{sd}(x)$.

The replays are spread over two forked processes with `parallel::mclapply()` (on
Windows they run serially). Each replay sets its own seed, so the results do not
depend on the number of processes.

```{r balance-replay}
n_proc = if (.Platform$OS.type == "unix") 2L else 1L
run_trial = function(design_class, X, y0, effect, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  d = design_class$new(n = nrow(X), response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
  for (t in seq_len(nrow(X))) {
    w_t = d$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[t, , drop = FALSE])
    d$add_one_subject_response(t, y0[t] + effect * w_t)
  }
  d
}
std_diff = function(d, X) {
  w = d$get_w()
  sapply(X, function(x) (mean(x[w == 1]) - mean(x[w == 0])) / sd(x))
}
designs = list(CR = DesignSeqOneByOneiBCRD, KK14 = DesignSeqOneByOneKK14,
               KK21 = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21)
n_replay = 100L
balance = lapply(designs, function(D) {
  do.call(rbind, parallel::mclapply(seq_len(n_replay), function(i)
    std_diff(run_trial(D, X, y0, true_effect, seed = 1000L + i), X), mc.cores = n_proc))
})
sapply(balance, function(b) round(sqrt(colMeans(b^2)), 3))   # RMS standardized difference
```

```{r balance-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
cols = c(CR = "darkorange", KK14 = "grey45", KK21 = "steelblue")
vals = list(); at = c(); k = 0
for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) for (nm in names(balance)) {
  k = k + 1
  vals[[k]] = abs(balance[[nm]][, j])
  at = c(at, (j - 1) * 4 + match(nm, names(balance)))
}
boxplot(vals, at = at, col = rep(cols, ncol(X)), xaxt = "n", outline = FALSE,
        ylim = c(0, 0.85),
        ylab = "|standardized difference in means|",
        main = sprintf("Covariate imbalance over %d replays of the same %d subjects", n_replay, n))
axis(1, at = (seq_len(ncol(X)) - 1) * 4 + 2,
     labels = c("x1 (strong)", "x2 (moderate)", "x3 (no effect)", "x4 (no effect)"))
legend("topright", bty = "n", fill = cols, cex = 0.85,
       legend = c("complete randomization (iBCRD)", "KK14", "KK21"))
```

```{r balance-numbers, include = FALSE}
rms = sapply(balance, function(b) sqrt(colMeans(b^2)))
ratio_x1_kk21 = rms["x1", "CR"] / rms["x1", "KK21"]
ratio_x1_kk14 = rms["x1", "CR"] / rms["x1", "KK14"]
```

By the root-mean-square standardized difference (printed above), both matching designs
are better balanced than complete randomization on every covariate, though on single
replays the distributions overlap a good deal. On `x1`, the root-mean-square standardized difference is
`r round(ratio_x1_kk14, 1)` times smaller under KK14 and `r round(ratio_x1_kk21, 1)`
times smaller under KK21 than under complete randomization. KK21 concentrates its
balance on `x1` and `x2`, the covariates its weights favor, and balances `x3` and `x4`
less tightly than KK14 does; those two covariates do not affect the outcome, so that
costs nothing.

## The estimator and its inference

A KK trial ends with two kinds of subjects: $m$ matched pairs and $n_R$ reservoir
subjects. The pairs give $m$ within-pair differences, treated minus control, each an
unbiased estimate of the treatment effect with most of the covariate noise removed.
The reservoir is a small completely randomized experiment of its own, which gives a
two-sample difference in means. Kapelner and Krieger (2014) combine the two with
inverse-variance weights,
$$\hat\beta_T = w^*\,\bar d + (1-w^*)\,\bar r, \qquad
  w^* = \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\bar r)}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\bar r) + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\bar d)},$$
where $\bar d$ is the mean pair difference and $\bar r$ is the reservoir difference in
means. When only one part is usable, the estimate falls back to that part.

EDI's recommended class for continuous outcomes, `InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik`, fits the
two parts as a single regression instead: it stacks the $m$ pair-difference rows
(response difference on covariate differences, with a unit treatment column) and the
$n_R$ reservoir rows (response on treatment and covariates) and fits one OLS. The
treatment coefficient is the estimate, and the standard errors use the HC2
heteroskedasticity-consistent sandwich, since pair differences and reservoir outcomes
need not have the same variance. By default it adjusts for the covariates in the
design's formula; pass `model_formula = ~ 1` to drop them. Because it is a full
Gaussian likelihood, the score and likelihood-ratio tests are available as well as
Wald.

```{r trial-inference}
inf = InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
inf$num_cores = 1L
inf$compute_estimate()
inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

**The randomization test.** `compute_rand_two_sided_pval()` redraws the assignment
from the design's own mechanism: each matched pair's treatments are swapped with
probability 1/2, and each reservoir subject is redrawn by a fair coin. Under the sharp
null hypothesis the responses do not change with the assignment, and neither KK14's
pairs (which depend only on the covariates) nor KK21's (whose weights regress the
response on each covariate without the treatment) depend on the assignment path, so
conditioning on the realized pairs is exact for these two designs.

```{r trial-rand}
inf$set_seed(1)
inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 200, show_progress = FALSE)
```

**No nonparametric bootstrap.** EDI does not offer the nonparametric bootstrap on
sequential designs: resampling subjects would not reproduce how the pairs and the
reservoir formed. The call stops with an error:

```{r trial-boot}
tryCatch(inf$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, B = 100, show_progress = FALSE),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

**Other continuous-outcome classes.** The reference index lists all of them; the ones
specific to KK designs are:

* `InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik`: the stacked OLS above (recommended).
* `InferenceContinKKRobustRegrOneLik`: the same stacked fit with robust regression,
  for heavy-tailed outcomes.
* `InferenceContinKKGLMM`: a linear mixed model with a random intercept per pair.
* `InferenceBaiAdjustedTKK14` and `InferenceBaiAdjustedTKK21`: the Bai, Romano and
  Shaikh adjusted $t$ variance for matched pairs, combined with the reservoir (these
  need the suggested package nbpMatching).
* `InferenceContinKKOLSIVWC`, `InferenceAllKKMeanDiffIVWC` and
  `InferenceAllKKWilcoxIVWC`: the inverse-variance-weighted combination (IVWC) of
  separate pair and reservoir fits; `InferenceAllKKMeanDiffIVWC` is the unadjusted
  estimator displayed above. These are legacy classes; use a `*OneLik` class for new
  analyses.

## Efficiency by simulation

How much does matching on the fly gain over randomizing each arrival? It depends on
how well the covariates predict the outcome. The simulation below runs two scenarios
with four standard-normal covariates and $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$ noise:

* **Prognostic covariates:** $y = 1.5\,x_1 + x_2 + \beta_T w + \varepsilon$. The
  covariates explain about three quarters of the outcome variance.
* **Uninformative covariates:** $y = \beta_T w + \varepsilon$. No covariate predicts
  the outcome.

Each scenario runs at $n = 40$ and $n = 100$ under three sequential designs
(complete randomization via `DesignSeqOneByOneiBCRD`, KK14 and KK21, all with default
settings) and two analyses each, with the effect fixed at $\beta_T = 0.5$:

* complete randomization: the difference in means
  (`InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar`) and covariate-adjusted OLS
  (`InferenceContinOLS`);
* KK14 and KK21: `InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik` without covariates
  (`model_formula = ~ 1`, so the only adjustment is the matching itself) and with
  them (the default).

For each combination we record the mean squared error (MSE) of the estimate and the
power of the Wald test at level 0.05.

```{r sim, message = FALSE}
beta_T = 0.5
ns = c(40L, 100L)
n_sim = 160L
outcome = list(prognostic    = function(X) 1.5 * X$x1 + 1.0 * X$x2,
               uninformative = function(X) rep(0, nrow(X)))

one_rep = function(i) {
  out = list()
  for (sc in names(outcome)) for (nn in ns) {
    set.seed(50000L + 1000L * nn + i)
    Xs = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(nn), x2 = rnorm(nn), x3 = rnorm(nn), x4 = rnorm(nn))
    y0s = outcome[[sc]](Xs) + rnorm(nn)
    for (dn in names(designs)) {
      d = run_trial(designs[[dn]], Xs, y0s, beta_T, seed = 70000L + 1000L * nn + i)
      infs = if (dn == "CR") {
        list(unadjusted = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(d, verbose = FALSE),
             adjusted   = InferenceContinOLS$new(d, verbose = FALSE))
      } else {
        list(unadjusted = InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik$new(d, model_formula = ~ 1, verbose = FALSE),
             adjusted   = InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik$new(d, verbose = FALSE))
      }
      for (an in names(infs)) {
        out[[length(out) + 1]] = data.frame(
          scenario = sc, n = nn, design = dn, analysis = an,
          est = infs[[an]]$compute_estimate(),
          pval = infs[[an]]$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval(),
          pairs = if (dn == "CR") NA_integer_ else max(d$get_block_ids()))
      }
    }
  }
  do.call(rbind, out)
}
sim_start = Sys.time()
sims = do.call(rbind, parallel::mclapply(seq_len(n_sim), one_rep, mc.cores = n_proc))
sim_secs = as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), sim_start, units = "secs"))

summ = do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sims, sims[, c("scenario", "n", "design", "analysis")],
                                   drop = TRUE), function(s) {
  se2 = (s$est - beta_T)^2
  pw = mean(s$pval < 0.05)
  data.frame(scenario = s$scenario[1], n = s$n[1], design = s$design[1],
             analysis = s$analysis[1], mse = mean(se2), mse_mcse = sd(se2) / sqrt(nrow(s)),
             power = pw, power_mcse = sqrt(pw * (1 - pw) / nrow(s)),
             mean_pairs = mean(s$pairs))
}))
rownames(summ) = NULL
summ$rel_eff = NA_real_                       # MSE of CR difference in means / this MSE
for (k in seq_len(nrow(summ))) {
  ref = summ$scenario == summ$scenario[k] & summ$n == summ$n[k] &
        summ$design == "CR" & summ$analysis == "unadjusted"
  summ$rel_eff[k] = summ$mse[ref] / summ$mse[k]
}
summ = summ[order(summ$scenario, summ$n, match(summ$design, names(designs)), summ$analysis), ]
fmt = transform(summ, mse = sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", mse, mse_mcse),
                power = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", power, power_mcse),
                rel_eff = round(rel_eff, 2), mean_pairs = round(mean_pairs, 1))
fmt[, c("scenario", "n", "design", "analysis", "mse", "rel_eff", "power", "mean_pairs")]
```

In the table, `mse` and `power` show the Monte Carlo standard error in parentheses,
`rel_eff` is the MSE of the unadjusted completely randomized analysis divided by the
row's MSE (above 1 means more efficient), and `mean_pairs` is the average number of
matched pairs.

```{r sim-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
for (sc in names(outcome)) {
  s = summ[summ$scenario == sc, ]
  ylim = c(0, max(s$mse + 2 * s$mse_mcse))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.6, 2.4), ylim = ylim, xaxt = "n", xlab = "sample size n",
       ylab = "MSE of the estimate", main = paste(sc, "covariates"))
  axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = ns)
  offs = c(CR = -0.2, KK14 = 0, KK21 = 0.2)
  for (dn in names(designs)) for (an in c("unadjusted", "adjusted")) {
    r = s[s$design == dn & s$analysis == an, ]
    r = r[order(r$n), ]
    x = match(r$n, ns) + offs[dn] + if (an == "adjusted") 0.05 else -0.05
    lines(x, r$mse, type = "b", col = cols[dn], pch = if (an == "adjusted") 17 else 19,
          lty = if (an == "adjusted") 2 else 1, lwd = 2)
    arrows(x, r$mse - 2 * r$mse_mcse, x, r$mse + 2 * r$mse_mcse,
           angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02, col = cols[dn])
  }
  if (sc == "prognostic")
    legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, col = c(cols, "black", "black"),
           lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2), pch = c(NA, NA, NA, 19, 17),
           legend = c("complete randomization", "KK14", "KK21",
                      "no covariate adjustment", "covariate-adjusted"))
}
```

```{r sim-numbers, include = FALSE}
get = function(sc, nn, dn, an, col) summ[summ$scenario == sc & summ$n == nn &
                                         summ$design == dn & summ$analysis == an, col]
re_kk21_u_40  = get("prognostic", 40, "KK21", "unadjusted", "rel_eff")
re_kk21_u_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK21", "unadjusted", "rel_eff")
re_kk14_u_40  = get("prognostic", 40, "KK14", "unadjusted", "rel_eff")
re_kk14_u_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK14", "unadjusted", "rel_eff")
pw_cr_u_100   = get("prognostic", 100, "CR", "unadjusted", "power")
pw_kk21_u_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK21", "unadjusted", "power")
pw_cr_a_40    = get("prognostic", 40, "CR", "adjusted", "power")
pw_kk21_a_40  = get("prognostic", 40, "KK21", "adjusted", "power")
re_un = summ$rel_eff[summ$scenario == "uninformative" & summ$design != "CR"]
mcse_pw_max = max(summ$power_mcse)
re_cr_a_100   = get("prognostic", 100, "CR", "adjusted", "rel_eff")
re_kk14_a_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK14", "adjusted", "rel_eff")
re_kk21_a_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK21", "adjusted", "rel_eff")
pw_cr_a_100   = get("prognostic", 100, "CR", "adjusted", "power")
pw_kk14_a_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK14", "adjusted", "power")
pw_kk21_a_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK21", "adjusted", "power")
pw_kk14_a_40  = get("prognostic", 40, "KK14", "adjusted", "power")
pairs_kk14_40  = get("prognostic", 40, "KK14", "adjusted", "mean_pairs")
pairs_kk21_40  = get("prognostic", 40, "KK21", "adjusted", "mean_pairs")
pairs_kk14_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK14", "adjusted", "mean_pairs")
pairs_kk21_100 = get("prognostic", 100, "KK21", "adjusted", "mean_pairs")
n_half_100 = 50
pw_un_40  = summ$power[summ$scenario == "uninformative" & summ$n == 40]
pw_un_100 = summ$power[summ$scenario == "uninformative" & summ$n == 100]
```

What the simulation shows (`r n_sim` simulated trials per cell; the largest Monte Carlo
standard error of a power estimate is `r round(mcse_pw_max, 3)`):

* **With prognostic covariates, matching alone recovers much of the precision.**
  Without any covariate adjustment in the analysis, KK21 is
  `r round(re_kk21_u_40, 1)` times as efficient as the completely randomized difference
  in means at $n = 40$ and `r round(re_kk21_u_100, 1)` times at $n = 100$ (KK14:
  `r round(re_kk14_u_40, 1)` and `r round(re_kk14_u_100, 1)`). At $n = 100$ the power
  rises from `r round(pw_cr_u_100, 2)` to `r round(pw_kk21_u_100, 2)`. KK21 forms more
  pairs than KK14 (on average `r round(pairs_kk21_100, 1)` vs.
  `r round(pairs_kk14_100, 1)` of the `r n_half_100` possible at $n = 100$), and spends
  them on the covariates that matter.
* **Covariate adjustment does most of the same work.** When the analysis also adjusts
  for the covariates, the designs end up close together. At $n = 100$ the relative
  efficiencies are `r round(re_cr_a_100, 1)` (complete randomization),
  `r round(re_kk14_a_100, 1)` (KK14) and `r round(re_kk21_a_100, 1)` (KK21), with
  power `r round(pw_cr_a_100, 2)`, `r round(pw_kk14_a_100, 2)` and
  `r round(pw_kk21_a_100, 2)`; the differences are about the size of the Monte Carlo
  error. At $n = 40$ the MSEs are again similar, but the adjusted KK analyses have
  *lower* power (`r round(pw_kk14_a_40, 2)` for KK14 and `r round(pw_kk21_a_40, 2)` for
  KK21, vs. `r round(pw_cr_a_40, 2)`): with only about `r round(pairs_kk14_40)` to
  `r round(pairs_kk21_40)` pairs, the stacked regression estimates the covariate
  slopes from few rows and its HC2 standard error is larger. Matching pays off most
  when the analysis is a simple comparison fixed in advance, and is not a substitute
  for adjustment in a small trial whose outcome model is known to be linear.
* **With uninformative covariates, matching buys nothing.** When no covariate predicts
  the outcome, the KK relative efficiencies range from `r round(min(re_un), 2)` to
  `r round(max(re_un), 2)`, and within each sample size the powers of all six analyses
  lie between `r round(min(pw_un_40), 2)` and `r round(max(pw_un_40), 2)` at $n = 40$
  and between `r round(min(pw_un_100), 2)` and `r round(max(pw_un_100), 2)` at
  $n = 100$, mostly within two Monte Carlo standard errors of each other. The matches
  are made on noise, so they cannot help.

One detail of the table: the covariate-adjusted analyses under complete randomization
and KK14 give exactly the same MSE in both scenarios. Neither design looks at the
response, both scenarios use the same covariates and noise, and a regression on the
covariates removes a linear covariate effect exactly, so the estimates are identical.
KK21's assignments depend on the responses, so its numbers differ between scenarios.

This is one data-generating process with linear covariate effects; the numbers are an
illustration, not a general rate. To size a real KK trial, simulate the outcome model
you expect with [Planning a Study](planning-a-study.html), which also covers
`SimulationFramework`.

## Other response types

The three KK designs accept every EDI response type (`"continuous"`, `"incidence"`,
`"proportion"`, `"count"`, `"survival"`, `"ordinal"`), and each type has inference
classes built for the pair-plus-reservoir structure. Some examples:

| Response type | KK inference classes |
|---|---|
| Incidence | `InferenceIncidKKCondLogitOneLik`, `InferenceIncidKKGCompRiskDiff`, `InferenceIncidKKModifiedPoisson` |
| Count | `InferenceCountKKCondPoissonOneLik`, `InferenceCountKKHurdlePoissonOneLik` |
| Proportion | `InferencePropKKGLMM`, `InferencePropKKGEE` |
| Survival | `InferenceSurvivalKKStratCoxPHOneLik`, `InferenceSurvivalKKLWACoxPHOneLik`, `InferenceSurvivalKKWeibullMarginal` |
| Ordinal | `InferenceOrdinalKKCLMM`, `InferenceOrdinalKKCondAdjCatLogitRegr` |

The workflow is the same as above; only the response and the inference class change.
For example, a binary outcome:

```{r incidence}
set.seed(7)
n_b = 80
Xb = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n_b), x2 = rnorm(n_b))
des_b = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(n = n_b, response_type = "incidence", verbose = FALSE)
for (t in seq_len(n_b)) {
  w_t = des_b$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(Xb[t, , drop = FALSE])
  p_t = plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * Xb$x1[t] + 0.8 * w_t)
  des_b$add_one_subject_response(t, rbinom(1, 1, p_t))
}
inf_b = InferenceIncidKKCondLogitOneLik$new(des_b, verbose = FALSE)
inf_b$num_cores = 1L
inf_b$compute_estimate()                            # log odds ratio
inf_b$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
```

`InferenceSuite` finds every class that applies to a given KK design and response
type and runs them together; see the [continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html).

## References

* Kapelner, A., and Krieger, A. M. (2014). Matching on-the-fly: Sequential allocation
  with higher power and efficiency. *Biometrics*, 70(2), 378–388.
  [doi:10.1111/biom.12148](https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.12148). The KK14 design and
  the inverse-variance combination of the matched-pair and reservoir estimates.
* Kapelner, A., and Krieger, A. M. (2021). The outcome-weighted extension of matching
  on the fly that `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21` and `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21stepwise`
  implement.
* Bai, Y., Romano, J. P., and Shaikh, A. M. (2021; in print 2022). Inference in experiments with
  matched pairs. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 117(540),
  1726–1737. The adjusted $t$ variance used by `InferenceBaiAdjustedTKK14` and
  `InferenceBaiAdjustedTKK21`.
